title: Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation
abstract: Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a new paradigm for sequential recommendation, in which a representative line of work encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and predicts the IDs token by token. However, this generative formulation still exhibits structural gaps with respect to the recommendation task: flattening multi-token IDs into a single sequence destroys item-level structure, and the inconsistency between training and inference over a hierarchical codebook gives rise to semantic drift. To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE, which employs Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding, and Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) together with Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from two complementary angles during decoding. Extensive experiments and analytical studies on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test demonstrate that BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform yields improvements of 0.60% in click-through rate, 1.34% in click unique visitors, and 1.70% in total reading time, confirming the practical value of BARGE in industrial-scale recommendation.

Abstract Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a new paradigm for sequential recommendation, in which a representative line of work encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and predicts the IDs token by token. However, this generative formulation still exhibits structural gaps with respect to the recommendation task: flattening multi-token IDs into a single sequence destroys item-level structure, and the inconsistency between training and inference over a hierarchical codebook gives rise to semantic drift . To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE , which employs Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding, and Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) together with Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from two complementary angles during decoding. Extensive experiments and analytical studies on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test demonstrate that BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform yields improvements of 0.60% in click-through rate, 1.34% in click unique visitors, and 1.70% in total reading time, confirming the practical value of BARGE in industrial-scale recommendation. I Introduction Figure 1: Two structural gaps in generative recommendation. Left (Item-Boundary Gap, P1): after each item is tokenized into L L hierarchical semantic IDs and flattened into a single sequence, item boundaries vanish from the input to the GR model, and the encoder can no longer tell which tokens belong to the same item (“Where is the item?”). Right (Semantic Drift, P2): on the hierarchical codebook tree, an error at any layer redirects decoding into a wrong subtree, so that the target leaf becomes unreachable along the chosen path no matter how the remaining tokens are scored. Sequential recommendation aims to predict the next item that a user will interact with, given the chronologically ordered history of past interactions. The dominant approach has long been discriminative. Models learn to score every candidate item against the encoded user history and select the highest-scoring ones. However, the per-item scoring nature of this paradigm causes its storage and computation costs to scale linearly with the size of the item set, which fundamentally limits its scalability. Generative approaches sidestep this bottleneck by directly producing item identifiers autoregressively. Generative Recommendation (GR) [ 8 , 12 , 37 , 34 , 21 , 15 ] offers a fundamentally different paradigm. Instead of scoring all candidates, GR generates the identifier of the target item token by token. To instantiate this generative idea, the mainstream practice [ 37 , 43 , 46 , 29 , 30 , 52 , 10 ] represents each item as a tuple of L L hierarchical semantic ID tokens ( c 1 , c 2 , … , c L ) (c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{L}) obtained via residual quantization methods such as RQ-VAE [ 41 , 25 ] . This formulation allows semantically similar items to share ID prefixes and reduces the inference complexity from linear in the size of the item set to logarithmic in the depth of the codebook. Despite this progress, the generative formulation was borrowed from natural language, where each token carries stand-alone lexical semantics. A hierarchical semantic codeword c l c_{l} , however, only acquires meaning when combined with its prefix c < l c_{<l} . This mismatch manifests as two structural gaps: (P1) Loss of item-level structure. Recommendation is fundamentally an item-level task, yet existing GR models decompose each item into L L semantic ID tokens and flatten all tokens into an undifferentiated sequence. The self-attention mechanism treats every token identically regardless of item membership, which effectively reduces item-level recommendation to token-level sequence modeling. As illustrated on the left of Fig. 1 , once items are flattened into a token sequence, the boundaries between items are no longer visible to the encoder, and tokens belonging to different items become indistinguishable from intra-item ones in terms of structural cues. Existing GR methods [ 37 , 43 , 46 ] universally adopt this flat-sequence strategy and leave item boundaries to be recovered implicitly from positional signals alone. (P2) Semantic drift in hierarchical decoding. Multi-level semantic IDs form a tree-like codebook in which the codeword selected at each layer constrains all subsequent layers, so that an error at any layer redirects the search into a wrong subtree. We refer to this family of failure modes collectively as semantic drift . As illustrated on the right of Fig. 1 , once decoding deviates from the correct branch, the target leaf is no longer reachable along the chosen path, while standard beam search keeps selecting codewords by locally normalized probabilities and is unaware of such cumulative drift. On TIGER, the per-layer accuracy of c 3 c_{3} drops from 77.0% (correct prefix) to 0.6% (erroneous prefix), a 128 × \times gap (Section V-F ). This drift can be attacked from two orthogonal angles: intra-path, by reranking candidates within a single channel via global path-level coherence; and cross-channel, by exposing the decoder to a second, structurally orthogonal quantization channel so that an item missed by one channel can still be recovered through the other via OR-style fusion. To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE ( B ridging A uto R egressive G eneration for r E commendation), with three lightweight modules: ICA closes the encoder-side gap (P1), while HPR and DPD jointly close the decoder-side drift gap (P2) from the two complementary angles above. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We formalise the long-standing semantic-fidelity gap of GR as two structural gaps along the GR pipeline: an encoder-side item-boundary gap, and a decoder-side semantic-drift gap. We further show that the latter can be mitigated from two complementary, orthogonal angles. • We propose BARGE with three lightweight and mutually orthogonal modules. ICA restores item-level structure at the encoder; HPR suppresses semantic drift via per-layer dual-tower contrastive reranking within a single decoding channel; and DPD further mitigates the same drift from a complementary angle via a Dual-Decoder coupled by an OSQ-VAE tokenizer. • Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. BARGE has also been deployed on Tencent’s commercial media platform, bringing consistent improvements across core engagement metrics in real-world industrial scenarios. II Related Work II-A Discriminative and Generative Recommendation Mainstream sequential recommendation methods are discriminative: they encode the interaction history into a user representation and score candidate items, with architectures evolving from RNN-based GRU4Rec [ 19 ] and CNN-based Caser [ 40 ] to Transformer-based SASRec [ 23 ] , BERT4Rec [ 38 ] , FDSA [ 50 ] , S 3 -Rec [ 53 ] , and more recent variants based on diffusion [ 28 ] , sparse attention [ 26 ] , and zero-shot transfer [ 3 ] . Despite their architectural diversity, these methods all rely on a candidate-scoring paradigm. Generative Recommendation (GR) [ 5 , 6 , 14 , 36 ] instead formulates recommendation as autoregressive generation of discrete item identifiers [ 8 , 12 , 7 , 27 , 1 , 51 ] . TIGER [ 37 ] established a representative framework that encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via RQ-VAE [ 25 ] , and subsequent work improves upon it through collaborative signals (LETTER [ 43 ] ), hybrid representations (COBRA [ 46 ] ), knowledge integration (MVIGER [ 24 ] ), and alternative indexing schemes [ 22 , 39 ] . More recently, HSTU [ 48 ] , OneRec [ 9 , 31 ] , RPG [ 20 ] , DACT [ 11 ] , DELRec [ 49 ] , and Reg4Rec [ 44 ] further advance GR through scalable architectures, end-to-end modeling, efficient generation, continual tokenization, knowledge distillation, and reasoning enhancement, respectively. Unlike Reg4Rec, the proposed DPD explicitly derives two complementary channels from a learnable orthogonal rotation of encoder features, providing a structural guarantee of channel diversity. II-B Structural Awareness and Semantic Drift Suppression Structural awareness in the encoding stage. When each item is decomposed into L L semantic ID tokens, the self-attention in the encoder treats all tokens as an undifferentiated flat sequence and consequently loses item-level grouping. In NLP, ALiBi [ 35 ] and Longformer [ 2 ] introduce structured attention via relative position bias and local-global patterns, but neither is tailored to semantic IDs. TrieRec [ 45 ] explores leveraging the prefix tree structure to introduce structural bias. Orthogonal to these efforts, the proposed ICA enriches every token with item-level semantics prior to encoding, via cross-attention pooling followed by a gated residual injection. Semantic drift suppression in hierarchical codebook decoding. Hierarchical semantic drift is inherent to any GR method that decodes multi-level semantic IDs, which distinguishes it from exposure bias in flat-vocabulary generation. Existing methods apply standard beam search without consistency-aware modification. PROMISE [ 13 ] explores applying the process reward idea from LLMs to rerank step-by-step decoding. APAO [ 47 ] addresses the gap between training and inference by introducing prefix-level pointwise and pairwise ranking losses together with an adaptive worst-prefix weighting strategy that aligns training with beam-search inference. In contrast, the proposed HPR is a lightweight, label-free auxiliary. At each decoder layer, it scores the semantic compatibility between the history-aggregated hidden state and the cumulative path embeddings via a dual-tower contrastive objective trained with symmetric InfoNCE. III Preliminary Let the user set be 𝒰 \mathcal{U} and the item set be 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . For a user u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} , the chronologically ordered historical interaction sequence is denoted as 𝐬 u = ( v 1 , v 2 , … , v T ) \mathbf{s}_{u}=(v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{T}) , where v t ∈ 𝒱 v_{t}\in\mathcal{V} . The goal is to predict the next item v T + 1 v_{T+1} . Semantic IDs via RQ-VAE. In the generative recommendation framework, each item v v is assigned a discrete semantic ID of length L L via Residual-Quantized VAE (RQ-VAE) [ 41 , 25 ] , which iteratively quantizes the residual of a pretrained item embedding across L L codebooks { 𝒞 l } l = 1 L \{\mathcal{C}_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} : v → 𝐬 ( v ) = ( c 1 ( v ) , c 2 ( v ) , … , c L ( v ) ) , v\;\rightarrow\;\mathbf{s}^{(v)}=(c_{1}^{(v)},\,c_{2}^{(v)},\,\dots,\,c_{L}^{(v)}), (1) where c l ( v ) ∈ 𝒞 l c_{l}^{(v)}\in\mathcal{C}_{l} is the codeword assigned at layer l l . Shallower layers capture coarse-grained semantic categories, whereas deeper layers progressively refine the representation within narrower subtrees. The codebook configuration and training details are discussed in Section V-H . Generative recommendation. The user history is represented as a flattened token sequence 𝐗 = [ 𝐬 ( v 1 ) ; ⋯ ; 𝐬 ( v T ) ] ∈ ℝ ( T ⋅ L ) × d \mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{s}^{(v_{1})};\cdots;\mathbf{s}^{(v_{T})}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(T\cdot L)\times d} , which is fed into an encoder [ 42 ] that produces the encoded history 𝐇 ∈ ℝ ( T ⋅ L ) × d \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{(T\cdot L)\times d} and autoregressively generates the target semantic ID of the next item: P ​ ( v T + 1 ∣ 𝐬 u ) = ∏ l = 1 L P l ​ ( c l ∣ c < l , 𝐇 ) , P(v_{T+1}\mid\mathbf{s}_{u})=\prod_{l=1}^{L}P_{l}\bigl(c_{l}\mid c_{<l},\,\mathbf{H}\bigr), (2) where 𝐇 \mathbf{H} is the encoder output and P l P_{l} is the decoder distribution over codebook 𝒞 l \mathcal{C}_{l} at decoding layer l l . IV Methodology IV-A Model Overview Figure 2: Overview of BARGE. (Top-left) The pretrained OSQ-VAE tokenizes each item into two channel-specific semantic-ID tuples (cbook_A and cbook_B) via orthogonal rotation and dual codebook stacks; the dual IDs are projected by an MLP into the flattened token sequence. (Top-middle) The user history passes through the ICA before the shared encoder. (Top-right) Two independent decoders (Channel A and Channel B) each followed by an HPR run in parallel; their Top- K K candidate lists are merged by OR-Fusion to produce the final recommendations. (Bottom-left) ICA: cross-attention pooling with a learnable query, MLP projection, and gated residual fusion. (Bottom-right) HPR: per-layer dual-tower scoring of cumulative path embeddings against the decoder hidden state h 0 h_{0} , trained with ℒ HPR \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HPR}} . As illustrated in Fig. 2 , BARGE addresses the two structural gaps identified in Section I with three modules: one that targets the encoder-side gap, and two complementary modules that jointly close the decoder-side drift gap. (1) Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) aggregates all token embeddings within each item into a single item-level context 𝐳 ( i ) \mathbf{z}^{(i)} and fuses it back into every token via a gating network before the encoder block, which closes the item-boundary gap (P1). (2) Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) augments beam search with per-layer dual-tower contrastive scoring trained via the symmetric InfoNCE loss ( ℒ HPR \mathcal{L}_{\text{HPR}} ) alongside the standard next-token prediction loss ( ℒ NTP \mathcal{L}_{\text{NTP}} ), in order to suppress the intra-path facet of decoder-side drift along a single quantization channel. (3) Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) replaces the single RQ-VAE tokenizer with an OSQ-VAE tokenizer. The OSQ-VAE decomposes the encoder feature into two complementary subspaces via a learnable orthogonal rotation R R , and emits two semantic-ID tuples per item. On top of a shared encoder, DPD runs a Dual-Decoder with channel-private HPR, and fuses their per-channel candidate items in the item-id space at inference time. In this way, the cross-channel facet of decoder-side drift is suppressed through orthogonal quantization channels. IV-B Structure-Aware Encoding via Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) ICA adopts an aggregate-then-fuse strategy (Fig. 2 , bottom-left): for each item, it first aggregates all token embeddings into a single item-level context, and then fuses this context back into every token via a gating network. Cross-attention pooling. Given the L L token embeddings { 𝐱 1 ( i ) , … , 𝐱 L ( i ) } \{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{(i)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(i)}\} of item v i v_{i} , ICA uses a learnable query vector 𝐪 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to compute the item-level context representation via cross-attention, in which 𝐪 \mathbf{q} serves as the query and the tokens of the item serve as the keys and values: 𝐳 ( i ) = LayerNorm ​ ( CrossAttn ​ ( 𝐪 , 𝐗 ( i ) , 𝐗 ( i ) ) ) , \mathbf{z}^{(i)}=\text{LayerNorm}\left(\text{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{q},\;\mathbf{X}^{(i)},\;\mathbf{X}^{(i)})\right), (3) where 𝐗 ( i ) = [ 𝐱 1 ( i ) ; … ; 𝐱 L ( i ) ] ∈ ℝ L × d \mathbf{X}^{(i)}=[\mathbf{x}_{1}^{(i)};\dots;\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(i)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} is the matrix of L L token embeddings for item v i v_{i} , and 𝐳 ( i ) ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{z}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the resulting item-level representation. Cross-attention is used here so that the learnable query 𝐪 \mathbf{q} can adaptively and dynamically weight the contribution of each token when forming the item-level context, since different layers of a semantic ID encode relative information at different granularities. Context projection. The context vector undergoes multi-layer nonlinear transformation: 𝐳 ^ ( i ) = W 2 ⋅ GELU ​ ( W 1 ⋅ 𝐳 ( i ) + 𝐛 1 ) + 𝐛 2 , \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}=W_{2}\cdot\text{GELU}(W_{1}\cdot\mathbf{z}^{(i)}+\mathbf{b}_{1})+\mathbf{b}_{2}, (4) where W 1 ∈ ℝ d f × d W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{f}\times d} , W 2 ∈ ℝ d × d f W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{f}} , d f d_{f} is the feed-forward hidden dimension, and 𝐳 ^ ( i ) ∈ ℝ d \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the projected context vector after the nonlinear transformation. Gated residual fusion. For each token l ∈ { 1 , … , L } l\in\{1,\dots,L\} of item v i v_{i} , a gating network controls how much item-level context is fused back into each token: 𝐠 l ( i ) = σ ​ ( W g ⋅ [ 𝐱 l ( i ) ∥ 𝐳 ^ ( i ) ] + 𝐛 g ) , \mathbf{g}_{l}^{(i)}=\sigma\left(W_{g}\cdot[\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(i)}\|\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}]+\mathbf{b}_{g}\right), (5) 𝐱 ^ l ( i ) = 𝐱 l ( i ) + 𝐠 l ( i ) ⊙ 𝐳 ^ ( i ) , \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(i)}=\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(i)}+\mathbf{g}_{l}^{(i)}\odot\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}, (6) where W g ∈ ℝ d × 2 ​ d W_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 2d} , 𝐠 l ( i ) ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{g}_{l}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the gate vector, σ ​ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, ∥ \| denotes concatenation, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The gated residual form allows each token to decide how much item-level context to admit, so that the injected context never overwhelms the positional and layer-specific information already encoded in 𝐱 l ( i ) \mathbf{x}_{l}^{(i)} . When the gate approaches zero, ICA reduces to the identity mapping and preserves the original token representation; when the gate approaches one, the token is fully merged with the item context. We empirically observe that the learned gate stabilises around 0.35 0.35 – 0.38 0.38 across all four layers (Section V-I ), which confirms that the network indeed learns a moderate and layer-consistent fusion strength. IV-C Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) HPR augments beam search with a per-layer reranking mechanism that evaluates the semantic compatibility between the initial hidden state of the decoder 𝐡 0 \mathbf{h}_{0} and the cumulative path embedding at each decoding layer (Fig. 2 , bottom-right). The key insight is that 𝐡 0 \mathbf{h}_{0} , produced by the cross-attention of the decoder over the full encoder output before any token is generated, serves as a holistic representation of the historical preferences of the user, which makes it a natural and suitable anchor for assessing whether a candidate path aligns with the intent of the user. Cumulative path embedding. Unlike token-level scoring that evaluates individual codewords in isolation, HPR operates explicitly at the path level to better capture dependencies between different layers. For each candidate at layer l l , the cumulative path embedding is computed as 𝐩 ( l ) = ∑ j = 1 l 𝐞 c j , \mathbf{p}^{(l)}=\sum_{j=1}^{l}\mathbf{e}_{c_{j}}, (7) where 𝐞 c j ∈ ℝ d emb \mathbf{e}_{c_{j}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{emb}}} is the learnable embedding of codeword c j c_{j} . This cumulative representation captures the semantic trajectory of the partial path and enables the reranker to assess global coherence rather than evaluating each token independently. Per-layer dual-tower scoring. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (bottom-right), HPR maintains a separate dual-tower scorer for each layer l l . Each scorer projects the initial hidden state of the decoder and the cumulative path embedding into a shared low-dimensional space, and then computes their cosine similarity scaled by a learnable temperature: r l ​ ( 𝐡 0 , 𝐩 ( l ) ) = cos ⁡ ( ϕ l ctx ​ ( 𝐡 0 ) , ϕ l path ​ ( 𝐩 ( l ) ) ) ⋅ e τ l , r_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{0},\mathbf{p}^{(l)})=\cos\!\bigl(\phi_{l}^{\text{ctx}}(\mathbf{h}_{0}),\;\phi_{l}^{\text{path}}(\mathbf{p}^{(l)})\bigr)\cdot e^{\tau_{l}}, (8) where ϕ l ctx : ℝ d attn → ℝ d proj \phi_{l}^{\text{ctx}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{attn}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{proj}}} and ϕ l path : ℝ d emb → ℝ d proj \phi_{l}^{\text{path}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{emb}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{proj}}} are layer-specific linear projections followed by L 2 L_{2} normalisation, and τ l \tau_{l} is the learnable log-temperature. The dual-tower architecture allows efficient scoring of multiple candidate paths, as the context projection is computed only once per sample. Training via symmetric InfoNCE. HPR is jointly trained with the main model using the InfoNCE loss. For each layer l l , within a batch of B B samples, the positive pair consists of the initial hidden state of the decoder 𝐡 0 ( i ) \mathbf{h}_{0}^{(i)} and the ground-truth cumulative path embedding 𝐩 ( l , i ) \mathbf{p}^{(l,i)} for sample i i . In addition to the in-batch negatives, we incorporate prefix-aware negatives that explicitly expose the model to plausible but erroneous prefixes. Concretely, at each decoding step, we draw high-probability candidates that are not ground truth from the NTP distribution, and further introduce business-level negatives such as impressed but unclicked items. These prefix-conditioned negatives emulate the drift patterns encountered during inference and strengthen the model’s ability to discriminate correct semantic prefixes from misleading or user-irrelevant ones. The per-layer loss is defined as ℒ HPR ( l ) = 1 2 ​ [ ℒ c2p ( l ) + ℒ p2c ( l ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{HPR}}^{(l)}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{c2p}}^{(l)}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{p2c}}^{(l)}\right], (9) where ℒ c2p ( l ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{c2p}}^{(l)} (context-to-path) and ℒ p2c ( l ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{p2c}}^{(l)} (path-to-context) are standard cross-entropy losses over the similarity matrix. The symmetric formulation ensures that both projection heads are well-calibrated: the context tower learns to produce representations that are discriminative across different paths, while the path tower learns representations that are discriminative across different user contexts. Joint scoring during inference. Standard beam search keeps a set of B B partial paths and, at layer l l , expands them into B × | 𝒞 l | B\times|\mathcal{C}_{l}| candidates scored solely by their cumulative log-probability; the top- B B are kept for the next layer. Such greedy local selection ignores global semantic coherence, and simply enlarging B B is costly, since the KV cache and the expanded score tensor all scale linearly with B B . We therefore follow prior generative works (e.g., B = 20 B=20 in TIGER [ 37 ] ) and instead correct erroneous paths without enlarging the beam. HPR intervenes after beam expansion at each layer. From the B × | 𝒞 l | B\times|\mathcal{C}_{l}| expanded candidates, we first keep the top- N N (with B < N ≪ B × | 𝒞 l | B<N\ll B\times|\mathcal{C}_{l}| ) ranked by generation log-probability to form a scoring pool, which retains semantically reasonable but locally lower-probability paths that vanilla beam search would prematurely discard. The top- B B paths under this fused score advance to layer l + 1 l{+}1 , so the outgoing beam width is unchanged and only a lightweight dual-tower scoring is added per layer, while the enlarged pool N N allows semantically inconsistent paths to be corrected before their errors propagate deeper. IV-D Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) ICA and HPR both operate within a single quantization channel, and neither addresses the cross-channel facet. A single RQ-VAE structure commits the decoder to one factorization of an item, projecting its rich semantics onto a single quantization axis; any semantic facet of the item not captured by that axis is permanently locked outside the corresponding semantic subtree. DPD tries to close this gap with three components: an OSQ-VAE tokenizer, a Dual-Decoder, and an OR-fusion inference procedure. OSQ-VAE (Orthogonal Split-and-Quantize VAE) tokenizer. Let 𝐳 ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{z}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{D} be the pretrained item embedding. The OSQ-VAE tokenizer first applies a learnable orthogonal rotation 𝐳 ~ = R ​ 𝐳 , R ∈ ℝ D × D , R ⊤ ​ R = I D , \tilde{\mathbf{z}}\;=\;R\,\mathbf{z},\qquad R\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D},\;\;R^{\top}R=I_{D}, (12) in which R R is parameterized as a product of Householder reflections, so that R ⊤ ​ R = I D R^{\top}R=I_{D} holds by construction throughout training without any auxiliary loss term. Inference: OR-fusion in the item-id space. At inference time, each decoder tower runs an independent beam search of width B B and produces a ranked list of channel-specific semantic IDs. These IDs are then mapped back to items via the OSQ-VAE codebook of the corresponding channel. Because each item carries two semantic IDs (one per channel), the two ranked lists live in the same item-id space and are merged by an OR-fusion operator: s ​ ( v ) = f ​ ( s ( A ) ​ ( v ) , s ( B ) ​ ( v ) ) , s(v)\;=\;f\!\bigl(s^{(A)}(v),\,s^{(B)}(v)\bigr), (17) where s ( c ) ​ ( v ) s^{(c)}(v) denotes the score of item v v under channel c c . An item is recovered as long as at least one channel ranks it highly, while items absent from both beams are uniformly rejected. This OR semantics directly attacks the cross-channel facet of semantic drift, and its effectiveness relies on the two channels proposing complementary top- K K candidates rather than on any postulated independence between them. We emphasize that OR-fusion does not enlarge the candidate budget: each tower still runs a beam of width B B identical to that of the single-tower baselines, and the merged ranked item list from which Recall@ K K and NDCG@ K K are computed is truncated at the same K K , so all reported metrics are evaluated under exactly the same protocol. V Experiment V-A Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate the proposed method on three datasets: (1) Amazon Beauty and (2) Amazon Sports and Outdoors, two widely used sequential recommendation benchmarks with 5-core filtering [ 18 ] ; and (3) a large-scale offline test from Tencent’s commercial media platform that comprises millions of users and hundreds of millions of interactions over 11 days (the first 10 days are used for training and the last day for evaluation).
